props.title: Spun
props.initialSlug: Meth addicts spiral through three frenzied days in LA

sections.content: Spun marked a frenetic entry into drug-fueled cinema, employing dizzying visuals and rapid-cut editing to simulate methamphetamine-induced mania. Director Jonas Åkerlund, known for music videos, brought his hyperkinetic style to this raw descent into addiction. The film follows Jason Schwartzman's character through a three-day meth binge, using over 5,000 edits and animated sequences to create a uniquely disorienting experience. While Requiem for a Dream (2000) approached addiction with haunting surrealism and Trainspotting (1996) balanced its darkness with dark humor, Spun took a more aggressive, almost assaultive approach to depicting drug culture.

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a shift in how films portrayed drug use, moving away from the glamorized excess of films like Scarface (1983) toward more visceral, consequence-heavy narratives. Party Monster (2003) and The Salton Sea (2002) specifically tackled methamphetamine culture, while Thirteen (2003) showed addiction's impact on youth. These films shared Spun's unflinching approach, though none matched its experimental visual assault. SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation in Drug Cinema

Spun's technical innovations influenced later drug-themed films like Enter the Void (2009) and Limitless (2011). Its rapid editing, extreme close-ups, and animated interludes created a new visual language for depicting altered states. Director Åkerlund's background in music videos for Prodigy and Madonna informed the film's style, while later works like Spring Breakers (2012) would adopt similar techniques to portray drug-induced experiences.
